Irreducibility of truncations of the Catalan generating functionThanks: This research was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP26K06734.

Shin-ichiro Seki Address: Nagahama Institute of Bio-Science and Technology, 1266, Tamura, Nagahama, Shiga, 526-0829, Japan Email address: s_seki@nagahama-i-bio.ac.jp
Abstract.

We prove that, for every positive integer nn, the polynomial

C0+C1​x+⋯+Cn​xnC_{0}+C_{1}x+\cdots+C_{n}x^{n}

is irreducible over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, where CkC_{k} denotes the kkth Catalan number.

Key words and phrases: 
Catalan numbers, irreducible polynomials, truncations of power series
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11R09; Secondary 11C08

1. Introduction

The Catalan numbers are defined by

Ck≔1k+1​(2​kk)C_{k}\coloneqq\frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}

for each nonnegative integer kk:

C0=1,C1=1,C2=2,C3=5,C4=14,C5=42,C6=132,C7=429,\displaystyle C_{0}=1,\quad C_{1}=1,\quad C_{2}=2,\quad C_{3}=5,\quad C_{4}=14,\quad C_{5}=42,\quad C_{6}=132,\quad C_{7}=429,
C8=1430,C9=4862,C10=16796,C11=58786,C12=208012,….\displaystyle C_{8}=1430,\quad C_{9}=4862,\quad C_{10}=16796,\quad C_{11}=58786,\quad C_{12}=208012,\quad\dots.

Their generating function is given by

∑k=0∞Ck​xk=1−1−4​x2​x\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}C_{k}x^{k}=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}

and has radius of convergence 1/41/4. For each nonnegative integer nn, we consider the degree nn truncation

Pn​(x)≔∑k=0nCk​xk∈ℤ⁡[x].P_{n}(x)\coloneqq\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}x^{k}\in\mathbb{Z}[x].

In this paper, we prove the following.

Theorem 1.1.

For every positive integer nn, the polynomial Pn​(x)P_{n}(x) is irreducible over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

This was conjectured by Zhi-Wei Sun on March 23, 2013, in OEIS A000108.

There are other known examples of formal power series whose nonconstant truncations are all irreducible over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. A classical example is the exponential series exp⁡(x)\exp(x).

Theorem 1.2 (Schur [5]).

For every positive integer nn, the polynomial

En​(x)≔1+x+x22!+⋯+xnn!E_{n}(x)\coloneqq 1+x+\frac{x^{2}}{2!}+\cdots+\frac{x^{n}}{n!}

is irreducible over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Schur not only proved the irreducibility of these polynomials but also determined their Galois groups.

Theorem 1.3 (Schur [6]).

For every positive integer nn, the Galois group of En​(x)E_{n}(x) over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is isomorphic to the alternating group AnA_{n} if nn is divisible by 44, and to the symmetric group SnS_{n} otherwise.

Coleman [1] gave an alternative proof of this theorem using Newton polygons.

Katz and Rivin [2] used Magma to carry out systematic computations of the Galois groups of truncations of a wide range of formal power series with rational coefficients. Among other results, they verified computationally that the Galois group of Pn​(x)P_{n}(x) over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is isomorphic to the symmetric group SnS_{n} for 1≤n≤20001\leq n\leq 2000; see [2, §4]. In particular, the irreducibility of Pn​(x)P_{n}(x) over ℚ\mathbb{Q} was already known in this range. Sun conjectured in OEIS A224416 that the Galois group of Pn​(x)P_{n}(x) over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is isomorphic to SnS_{n} for every positive integer nn. We do not address this stronger conjecture in the present paper.

2. Nuts and bolts

In this section, we prepare two tools for use later in the proof. For each nonnegative integer nn, define the monic polynomial Qn​(x)∈ℤ​[x]Q_{n}(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x] by

Qn​(x)≔xn​Pn​(1/x)=∑k=0nCk​xn−k.Q_{n}(x)\coloneqq x^{n}P_{n}(1/x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}C_{k}x^{n-k}.

Since Pn​(x)P_{n}(x) is irreducible over ℚ\mathbb{Q} if and only if Qn​(x)Q_{n}(x) is, we work with Qn​(x)Q_{n}(x) in what follows.

2.1. Location of the roots of Qn​(x)Q_{n}(x)

For each positive integer nn, define

Δn≔(318)n+1+∑j=1n6​Cn−jn−j+2​(318)j.\Delta_{n}\coloneqq\left(\frac{31}{8}\right)^{n+1}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{6C_{n-j}}{n-j+2}\left(\frac{31}{8}\right)^{j}.
Lemma 2.1.

For every n≥320n\geq 320, Δn<4​Cn\Delta_{n}<4C_{n}.

Proof.

For n≥320n\geq 320, we have Cn+1/Cn≥641/161C_{n+1}/C_{n}\geq 641/161, which implies

318​(8​Cn−Cn+1)<4​Cn+1.\frac{31}{8}(8C_{n}-C_{n+1})<4C_{n+1}.

Thus, the identity

Δn+1=318​Δn+318​(4​Cn−Cn+1)\Delta_{n+1}=\frac{31}{8}\Delta_{n}+\frac{31}{8}(4C_{n}-C_{n+1})

shows that Δn<4​Cn\Delta_{n}<4C_{n} implies Δn+1<4​Cn+1\Delta_{n+1}<4C_{n+1}. Therefore, it remains to verify that Δ320<4​C320\Delta_{320}<4C_{320}. This can be checked numerically; in fact, Δ320/(4​C320)=0.99325275​…\Delta_{320}/(4C_{320})=0.99325275\dots. ∎

This inequality does not hold for n=319n=319. In fact, Δ319/(4​C319)=1.01582917​…\Delta_{319}/(4C_{319})=1.01582917\dots.

Proposition 2.2.

Let n≥320n\geq 320. Then every complex root α\alpha of Qn​(x)Q_{n}(x) satisfies

318<|α|≤4−6n+1<4.\frac{31}{8}<|\alpha|\leq 4-\frac{6}{n+1}<4.
Proof.

The upper bound follows from the Eneström–Kakeya theorem, since

CkCk−1=2​(2​k−1)k+1=4−6k+1≤4−6n+1\frac{C_{k}}{C_{k-1}}=\frac{2(2k-1)}{k+1}=4-\frac{6}{k+1}\leq 4-\frac{6}{n+1}

for 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. To prove the lower bound, suppose that Qn​(x)Q_{n}(x) has a root α\alpha with |α|≤31/8|\alpha|\leq 31/8. Since

(4−x)​Qn​(x)=4​Cn+∑j=1n6​Cn−jn−j+2​xj−xn+1,(4-x)Q_{n}(x)=4C_{n}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{6C_{n-j}}{n-j+2}x^{j}-x^{n+1},

we have

4​Cn=αn+1−∑j=1n6​Cn−jn−j+2​αj.4C_{n}=\alpha^{n+1}-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{6C_{n-j}}{n-j+2}\alpha^{j}.

By the triangle inequality, we obtain 4​Cn≤Δn4C_{n}\leq\Delta_{n}, contradicting Lemma 2.1. ∎

2.2. A lower bound for a product of primes

For each positive integer nn, define

Πn≔∏n+1<p≤2​np: primep.\Pi_{n}\coloneqq\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}n+1<p\leq 2n\\ p:\text{ prime}\end{subarray}}p.
Proposition 2.3.

For n≥320n\geq 320, we have Πn>26​n/5\Pi_{n}>2^{6n/5}.

Proof.

Let ϑ⁡(x)\vartheta(x) denote the first Chebyshev function, defined by

ϑ⁡(x)≔∑p≤xlog⁡p.\vartheta(x)\coloneqq\sum_{p\leq x}\log p.

Rosser and Schoenfeld [4, Theorem 4] proved that

|ϑ⁡(x)−x|≤x2​log⁡x|\vartheta(x)-x|\leq\frac{x}{2\log x}

for x≥563x\geq 563. Since log⁡Πn=ϑ⁡(2​n)−ϑ⁡(n+1)\log\Pi_{n}=\vartheta(2n)-\vartheta(n+1), we can use this estimate, together with some numerical computations, to obtain the desired inequality. ∎

3. Reduction to a functional equation

Since the irreducibility of Qn​(x)Q_{n}(x) has been verified computationally for 1≤n<3201\leq n<320, it suffices to consider the case n≥320n\geq 320. Suppose, for a contradiction, that Qn​(x)Q_{n}(x) is reducible over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. By Gauss’s lemma, we may write Qn​(x)=F⁡(x)​G​(x)Q_{n}(x)=F(x)G(x) with nonconstant monic polynomials F⁡(x),G⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]F(x),G(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]. The following claim plays a key role in the proof and will be proved in the next section.

Claim 3.1 (Forced functional equation).

After interchanging F⁡(x)F(x) and G⁡(x)G(x) if necessary, we have

(3.1) F⁡(4−x)=(−1)deg⁡F​F​(x).F(4-x)=(-1)^{\deg F}F(x).

Let W⁡(x)≔x2−4​x+16W(x)\coloneqq x^{2}-4x+16, and let α\alpha be a root of FF. Claim 3.1 implies that 4−α4-\alpha is also a root of FF. Set a≔16−|α|2a\coloneqq 16-|\alpha|^{2} and b≔16−|4−α|2b\coloneqq 16-|4-\alpha|^{2}. By Proposition 2.2, we have 0<a,b<10<a,b<1. A direct calculation shows that

|W⁡(α)|2=a2−a​b+b2,|W(\alpha)|^{2}=a^{2}-ab+b^{2},

and hence |W⁡(α)|<1|W(\alpha)|<1.

Every root of F⁡(x)F(x) has absolute value less than 44, whereas the roots 2±2​3​i2\pm 2\sqrt{3}i of W⁡(x)W(x) have absolute value 44. Thus, F⁡(x)F(x) and W⁡(x)W(x) have no common root. Let α1,…,αdeg⁡F\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{\deg F} be the roots of FF, counted with multiplicity (in fact, all roots are simple). Since F⁡(x)F(x) is monic, we obtain

0<|Res⁡(F,W)|=∏i=1deg⁡F|W⁡(αi)|<1.0<|\Res(F,W)|=\prod_{i=1}^{\deg F}|W(\alpha_{i})|<1.

Here, Res⁡(F,W)\Res(F,W) denotes the resultant of F⁡(x)F(x) and W⁡(x)W(x). On the other hand, since F⁡(x),W⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]F(x),W(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x], we have Res⁡(F,W)∈ℤ\Res(F,W)\in\mathbb{Z}, a contradiction. This reduces the proof of Theorem 1.1 to Claim 3.1.

4. Proof of the claim

4.1. Local functional equation

For each prime pp and each polynomial f⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x], let f¯​(x)∈𝔽p​[x]\overline{f}(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x] denote its reduction modulo pp. In this subsection, all roots are taken in an algebraic closure 𝔽p¯\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}} of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}.

Let n≥320n\geq 320, and let pp be a prime satisfying n+1<p≤2​nn+1<p\leq 2n. Since p|Ckp\mid C_{k} for p+12≤k≤n\frac{p+1}{2}\leq k\leq n, we have

(4.1) Qn¯​(x)=xn−p−12​Qp−12¯​(x).\overline{Q_{n}}(x)=x^{n-\frac{p-1}{2}}\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}(x).

For 0≤k≤p−120\leq k\leq\frac{p-1}{2}, the congruence

2​Ck≡−(−4)k+1​(p+12k+1)(modp)2C_{k}\equiv-(-4)^{k+1}\binom{\frac{p+1}{2}}{k+1}\pmod{p}

holds, and hence

2​Qp−12¯​(x)=xp+12−(x−4)p+12.2\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}(x)=x^{\frac{p+1}{2}}-(x-4)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}.

This can also be deduced from Mattarei and Tauraso’s result [3, Theorem 3]. It follows that

Qp−12¯​(x)​(xp+12+(x−4)p+12)=2​(xp+x−4).\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}(x)\bigl(x^{\frac{p+1}{2}}+(x-4)^{\frac{p+1}{2}}\bigr)=2(x^{p}+x-4).

Therefore,

Qp−12¯|xp+x−4\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}\mid x^{p}+x-4

in 𝔽p​[x]\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]. Since the derivative of xp+x−4x^{p}+x-4 is 11, this polynomial has no multiple roots.

Lemma 4.1.

Let U​(x)∈𝔽p​[x]U(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x] be any monic divisor of Qp−12¯​(x)\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}(x). Let γ1,…,γdeg⁡U\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{\deg U} be the roots of U⁡(x)U(x). Then

(4.2) U⁡(4−x)=(−1)deg⁡U​U​(x)U(4-x)=(-1)^{\deg U}U(x)

and

(4.3) ∑i=1deg⁡Uγi=2​deg⁡U.\sum_{i=1}^{\deg U}\gamma_{i}=2\deg U.
Proof.

Let γ\gamma be a root of UU. Since U​(x)∈𝔽p​[x]U(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x], we have

U⁡(γp)=U​(γ)p=0.U(\gamma^{p})=U(\gamma)^{p}=0.

Moreover, U⁡(x)|xp+x−4U(x)\mid x^{p}+x-4 implies that γp=4−γ\gamma^{p}=4-\gamma. Thus, 4−γ4-\gamma is also a root of U⁡(x)U(x). Since the map γ↦4−γ\gamma\mapsto 4-\gamma is an involution, it permutes the roots of UU. Thus,

U⁡(4−x)\displaystyle U(4-x) =∏i=1deg⁡U(4−x−γi)=(−1)deg⁡U​∏i=1deg⁡U(x−(4−γi))\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{\deg U}(4-x-\gamma_{i})=(-1)^{\deg U}\prod_{i=1}^{\deg U}\bigl(x-(4-\gamma_{i})\bigr)
=(−1)deg⁡U​∏i=1deg⁡U(x−γi)=(−1)deg⁡U​U​(x).\displaystyle=(-1)^{\deg U}\prod_{i=1}^{\deg U}(x-\gamma_{i})=(-1)^{\deg U}U(x).

Moreover,

∑i=1deg⁡Uγi=∑i=1deg⁡U(4−γi)=4​deg⁡U−∑i=1deg⁡Uγi.\sum_{i=1}^{\deg U}\gamma_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{\deg U}(4-\gamma_{i})=4\deg U-\sum_{i=1}^{\deg U}\gamma_{i}.

Since pp is odd, this gives (4.3). ∎

4.2. Lifting the local functional equations

As in Section 3, let n≥320n\geq 320, and suppose that Qn​(x)=F⁡(x)​G​(x)Q_{n}(x)=F(x)G(x) with nonconstant monic polynomials F⁡(x),G⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[x]F(x),G(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]. Let α1,…,αdeg⁡F\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{\deg F} and β1,…,βdeg⁡G\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{\deg G} be the complex roots of F⁡(x)F(x) and G⁡(x)G(x), respectively, counted with multiplicity. Set

deg^​F≔2​deg⁡F−∑i=1deg⁡Fαi,deg^​G≔2​deg⁡G−∑j=1deg⁡Gβj.\widehat{\deg}\,F\coloneqq 2\deg F-\sum_{i=1}^{\deg F}\alpha_{i},\quad\widehat{\deg}\,G\coloneqq 2\deg G-\sum_{j=1}^{\deg G}\beta_{j}.

Since F⁡(x)F(x) and G⁡(x)G(x) are monic with integer coefficients, their sums of roots, and hence deg^​F\widehat{\deg}\,F and deg^​G\widehat{\deg}\,G, are integers.

Claim 4.2.

Let pp be a prime satisfying n+1<p≤2​nn+1<p\leq 2n. If p∤F⁡(0)p\nmid F(0), then

deg^​F≡0(modp),\widehat{\deg}\,F\equiv 0\pmod{p},

whereas if p|F⁡(0)p\mid F(0), then

deg^​F≡2​n+1(modp).\widehat{\deg}\,F\equiv 2n+1\pmod{p}.

The same assertion holds for GG.

Proof.

If p∤F⁡(0)p\nmid F(0), then (4.1) implies that F¯​(x)|Qp−12¯​(x)\overline{F}(x)\mid\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}(x). Hence, by (4.3), we obtain

∑i=1deg⁡Fαi≡the sum of the roots of ​F¯​(x)=2​deg⁡F¯=2​deg⁡F(modp),\sum_{i=1}^{\deg F}\alpha_{i}\equiv\text{the sum of the roots of }\overline{F}(x)=2\deg\overline{F}=2\deg F\pmod{p},

which gives deg^​F≡0(modp)\widehat{\deg}\,F\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

If p|F⁡(0)p\mid F(0), then p∤G⁡(0)p\nmid G(0), since F⁡(0)​G​(0)=CnF(0)G(0)=C_{n} is divisible by pp but not by p2p^{2}. Thus, xn−p−12|F¯​(x)x^{n-\frac{p-1}{2}}\mid\overline{F}(x), and we may write F¯​(x)=xn−p−12​U​(x)\overline{F}(x)=x^{n-\frac{p-1}{2}}U(x), where U​(x)∈𝔽p​[x]U(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[x] is monic and satisfies U​(x)|Qp−12¯​(x)U(x)\mid\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}(x). Since deg⁡U=deg⁡F−n+p−12\deg U=\deg F-n+\frac{p-1}{2}, it follows from (4.3) that

∑i=1deg⁡Fαi≡the sum of the roots of ​U​(x)=2​deg⁡U≡2​deg⁡F−2​n−1(modp),\sum_{i=1}^{\deg F}\alpha_{i}\equiv\text{the sum of the roots of }U(x)=2\deg U\equiv 2\deg F-2n-1\pmod{p},

which gives deg^​F≡2​n+1(modp)\widehat{\deg}\,F\equiv 2n+1\pmod{p}. ∎

Claim 4.2 gives

(4.4) Πn|deg^​F​(2​n+1−deg^​F).\Pi_{n}\mid\widehat{\deg}\,F\ \bigl(2n+1-\widehat{\deg}\,F\bigr).

After interchanging F⁡(x)F(x) and G⁡(x)G(x) if necessary, we may first assume that deg⁡F≤n/2\deg F\leq n/2. Since |αi|<4|\alpha_{i}|<4 by Proposition 2.2, we have

|∑i=1deg⁡Fαi|<4​deg⁡F≤2​n.\left|\sum_{i=1}^{\deg F}\alpha_{i}\right|<4\deg F\leq 2n.

Thus, −n<deg^​F<3​n-n<\widehat{\deg}\,F<3n, and Proposition 2.3 yields

|deg^​F​(2​n+1−deg^​F)|<3​n​(n+1)<26​n/5<Πn.|\widehat{\deg}\,F\ (2n+1-\widehat{\deg}\,F)|<3n(n+1)<2^{6n/5}<\Pi_{n}.

Combining this estimate with the divisibility relation (4.4), we obtain deg^​F​(2​n+1−deg^​F)=0\widehat{\deg}\,F\ (2n+1-\widehat{\deg}\,F)=0. Hence, either deg^​F=0\widehat{\deg}\,F=0 or deg^​F=2​n+1\widehat{\deg}\,F=2n+1. Since deg⁡F+deg⁡G=n\deg F+\deg G=n and

∑i=1deg⁡Fαi+∑j=1deg⁡Gβj=−C1=−1,\sum_{i=1}^{\deg F}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{\deg G}\beta_{j}=-C_{1}=-1,

we have deg^​F+deg^​G=2​n+1\widehat{\deg}\,F+\widehat{\deg}\,G=2n+1. Thus, if deg^​F=0\widehat{\deg}\,F=0, then deg^​G=2​n+1\widehat{\deg}\,G=2n+1, whereas if deg^​F=2​n+1\widehat{\deg}\,F=2n+1, then deg^​G=0\widehat{\deg}\,G=0. Consequently, after interchanging F⁡(x)F(x) and G⁡(x)G(x) once more if necessary, we may assume that

deg^​F=0,deg^​G=2​n+1.\widehat{\deg}\,F=0,\qquad\widehat{\deg}\,G=2n+1.

We now prove (3.1) for this choice of FF.

If pp is a prime divisor of Πn\Pi_{n}, then p∤2​n+1p\nmid 2n+1, since p<2​n+1<2​pp<2n+1<2p. By Claim 4.2, we have p|G⁡(0)p\mid G(0) for every such pp, and hence Πn|G⁡(0)\Pi_{n}\mid G(0). Moreover, G⁡(0)≠0G(0)\neq 0 since F⁡(0)​G​(0)=Cn≠0F(0)G(0)=C_{n}\neq 0. By Proposition 2.2 and Proposition 2.3, we obtain

4deg⁡G>|G⁡(0)|≥Πn>43​n/5.4^{\deg G}>|G(0)|\geq\Pi_{n}>4^{3n/5}.

It follows that deg⁡G>3​n/5\deg G>3n/5, and hence deg⁡F<2​n/5\deg F<2n/5.

Set

H⁡(x)≔F⁡(x+2)=xdeg⁡F+a1​xdeg⁡F−1+⋯+adeg⁡F−1​x+adeg⁡F.H(x)\coloneqq F(x+2)=x^{\deg F}+a_{1}x^{\deg F-1}+\cdots+a_{\deg F-1}x+a_{\deg F}.

It remains to prove that H⁡(−x)=(−1)deg⁡F​H​(x)H(-x)=(-1)^{\deg F}H(x), which is equivalent to showing that ai=0a_{i}=0 for every odd ii with 1≤i≤deg⁡F1\leq i\leq\deg F.

Let pp be a prime divisor of Πn\Pi_{n}. By Claim 4.2, we have p∤F⁡(0)p\nmid F(0), and hence F¯​(x)|Qp−12¯​(x)\overline{F}(x)\mid\overline{Q_{\frac{p-1}{2}}}(x). It follows from (4.2) that H¯​(−x)=(−1)deg⁡F​H¯​(x)\overline{H}(-x)=(-1)^{\deg F}\overline{H}(x). Since pp is odd, this implies that ai≡0(modp)a_{i}\equiv 0\pmod{p} for every odd ii. Thus, Πn|ai\Pi_{n}\mid a_{i} for every odd ii. By Proposition 2.2, every root of H⁡(x)H(x) has absolute value less than 66. Hence, using Proposition 2.3, we obtain

|ai|<(deg⁡Fi)​6i<(1+6)deg⁡F<72​n/5<26​n/5<Πn.|a_{i}|<\binom{\deg F}{i}6^{i}<(1+6)^{\deg F}<7^{2n/5}<2^{6n/5}<\Pi_{n}.

Therefore, ai=0a_{i}=0 for every odd ii with 1≤i≤deg⁡F1\leq i\leq\deg F. This proves Claim 3.1 and completes the proof of Theorem 1.1.
